BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- The commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia's Force 47 told reporters in Bogota Monday -- a day after surrendering -- that "the solution is not through war. There must be dialogue." Nelly Avila Moreno, center, alias Karina, is escorted by soldiers after surrendering. Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, whose nom de guerre was Karina, said she and her longtime male companion made the decision jointly to abandon the FARC group, based in the jungle, at 5 a.m. Sunday. She said pressure from Colombian soldiers had been key to their decision, and she called on her fellow rebels to follow her example. "I invite them to change the sensibility that is among the guerrillas," she said, seated by her companion, who said nothing during the news conference. She also had a message for the Colombian people: "It is important to do something for peace in Colombia, and that need to do something is precisely one of my motivations." After 24 years with the FARC, Karina said she wants to reintegrate with society. "At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with all of society," she said. Karina said she had had no contact with the group's leaders for the past two years. During that time, she said, "I was trying to stay alive." She said she knows nothing about the group's leaders, because "everything in the FARC is very compartmentalized." Still, she did hear through the news media about the killing by another member of FARC of Ivan Rios, a member of the group's central high command. "We suffered a very strong blow," she said. She acknowledged that news led her to worry about the possibility that one of her fellow guerrillas might consider doing the same thing to her. "A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don't know what each one is thinking," she said. Asked about news reports of guerrilla operations she may have participated in, Karina admitted to nothing. "They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn't part of," she said. But Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Espanol that he remembers well the woman who, with a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was on in 2004 in northwest Colombia, ordered him and the other passengers off and the bus be burned. "The commander of that guerrilla group -- a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing -- called herself Karina," he said. "She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles and I remained castrated for all my life." Asked specifically about the killing of the father of President Alvaro Uribe in 1983, she said she did not know who carried out the act, and added, "I don't have my hands stained in that deed." She said that with her surrender have come new fears about possible retribution from FARC loyalists, who consider her a traitor. Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, she said she once believed the FARC would rule Colombia. "I once dreamed of that," she said. Gen. Mario Montoya, chief of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were sent Sunday to pick up Karina and her companion, who had given authorities their general location. "With this, we have given a confounding strike to the FARC structure," particularly to Front 47, which at this point is practically dismantled," he said. Since the killing of Rios, 45 members of the group have laid down their arms and accepted a government plan for reinstallation into society, he said. "We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains," he said. "To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don't, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don't want them dead. We want them alive."

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) — The commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia’s Force 47 told reporters in Bogota on Monday—one day after surrendering—that “the solution is not through war. There must be dialogue.”

Nelly Avila Moreno, 45, known by the nom de guerre Karina, was escorted by soldiers after surrendering. She said she and her longtime male companion jointly decided to abandon the FARC, a jungle-based guerrilla group, at 5 a.m. Sunday.

Karina said pressure from Colombian soldiers had been a key factor in their decision, and she urged her fellow rebels to follow her example.

“I invite them to change the sensibility that is among the guerrillas,” she said, seated beside her companion, who remained silent during the news conference.

She also had a message for the Colombian people: “It is important to do something for peace in Colombia, and that need to do something is precisely one of my motivations.”

After 24 years with the FARC, Karina said she now wants to reintegrate into society.

“At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with all of society,” she said.

Karina said she had had no contact with the group’s leaders for the past two years. During that time, she said, “I was trying to stay alive.”

She said she knows nothing about the group’s leaders because “everything in the FARC is very compartmentalized.” Still, she said she learned through the news media about the killing of Ivan Rios, a member of the group’s central high command, by another FARC member.

“We suffered a very strong blow,” she said.

She acknowledged that the news made her fear that one of her fellow guerrillas might consider doing the same to her.

“A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don’t know what each one is thinking,” she said.

Asked about news reports regarding guerrilla operations in which she may have participated, Karina admitted to nothing.

“They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn’t part of,” she said.

But Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Español that he clearly remembers the woman who, accompanied by a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was riding in 2004 in northwestern Colombia, ordered him and the other passengers off, and ordered the bus to be burned.

“The commander of that guerrilla group—a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing—called herself Karina,” he said. “She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles and I remained castrated for all my life.”

Asked specifically about the 1983 killing of the father of President Alvaro Uribe, Karina said she did not know who carried out the act, adding, “I don’t have my hands stained in that deed.”

She said her surrender has brought new fears of possible retribution from FARC loyalists, who consider her a traitor.

Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, Karina said she once believed the FARC would rule Colombia.

“I once dreamed of that,” she said.

Gen. Mario Montoya, chief of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were sent Sunday to pick up Karina and her companion after they provided authorities with their general location.

“With this, we have given a confounding strike to the FARC structure,” particularly to Front 47, “which at this point is practically dismantled,” he said.

Since the killing of Rios, 45 members of the group have laid down their arms and accepted a government plan for reintegration into society, Montoya said.

“We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains,” he said. “To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don’t, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don’t want them dead. We want them alive.”

Karina also addressed Colombians more broadly, saying, “It is important to do something for peace in Colombia, and that need to do something is precisely one of my motivations.”

After spending 24 years in the FARC, she said her goal now is to return to civilian life. “At this moment, what I am thinking about is reuniting with my family and with all of society,” she said.

Karina said she had not communicated with FARC leaders for the previous two years. During that period, she said, “I was trying to stay alive.” She added that she had no information about the organization’s leadership because “everything in the FARC is very compartmentalized.”

Even so, she said she learned through media reports that Ivan Rios, a member of the FARC’s central high command, had been killed by another FARC member. “We suffered a very strong blow,” she said. She admitted that the news made her fear that another guerrilla might consider doing the same to her. “A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don’t know what each one is thinking,” she said.

When asked about reports linking her to guerrilla actions, Karina did not acknowledge involvement in any of them. “They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn’t part of,” she said.

However, Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Español that he clearly remembered a woman who, along with a group of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was riding in northwestern Colombia in 2004. He said the passengers were forced off and the bus was ordered burned.

“The commander of that guerrilla group — a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing — called herself Karina,” Paez said. “She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles and I remained castrated for all my life.”

Asked directly about the 1983 killing of President Alvaro Uribe’s father, Karina said she did not know who was responsible. “I don’t have my hands stained in that deed,” she added.

She also said that surrendering had created new fears for her, including the possibility of retaliation from FARC loyalists who view her as a traitor.

Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, Karina said she had once believed the FARC would eventually govern Colombia. “I once dreamed of that,” she said.

Gen. Mario Montoya, the head of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were dispatched Sunday to collect Karina and her companion after they provided authorities with their approximate location.

“With this, we have given a confounding strike to the FARC structure,” Montoya said, especially to Front 47, which he described as nearly dismantled.

He said that since Rios was killed, 45 members of the organization had given up their weapons and entered a government program intended to help them return to society.

“We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains,” Montoya said. “To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don’t, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don’t want them dead. We want them alive.”

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — A senior commander of Colombia’s FARC guerrilla movement, Nelly Ávila Moreno — better known by her nom de guerre, **“Karina”** — has surrendered to authorities, marking a significant symbolic blow to the rebel group and adding momentum to calls for a negotiated end to decades of conflict.

Ávila Moreno, once one of the most feared commanders in the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, turned herself in amid intensifying military pressure on the insurgency. Colombian officials presented her surrender as evidence that the FARC’s leadership was weakening after a series of major setbacks.

Speaking after laying down her weapon, Karina called for an end to the fighting and urged remaining guerrillas to seek a political solution.

“The path is dialogue, not war,” she said in comments carried by Colombian media, appealing to fighters still in the jungle to consider surrendering and rejoining civilian life.

Karina had long operated in western Colombia and was accused by authorities of involvement in kidnappings, attacks on security forces and other crimes linked to the FARC’s armed campaign. Her surrender was seen as especially important because of her rank and notoriety within the guerrilla organization.

Colombia’s government said her decision demonstrated the effectiveness of its demobilization program, which offers reduced penalties and support to rebels who abandon the armed struggle. Officials also urged other members of the FARC to follow her example.

The FARC, founded in the 1960s as a Marxist insurgency, financed much of its war through kidnapping, extortion and the drug trade, according to Colombian and U.S. authorities. The conflict involving guerrillas, paramilitary groups and state forces left hundreds of thousands dead or displaced over several decades.

Karina’s surrender came during a period of mounting pressure on the rebel group, which had recently lost several top figures to military operations and internal turmoil. Analysts said her defection reflected declining morale within FARC ranks and growing difficulty maintaining control over remote units.

For many Colombians, her public appeal carried weight precisely because it came from a commander once deeply embedded in the conflict.

“I invite my comrades to think of their families, to think of Colombia, and to give peace a chance,” she said.

While her surrender did not end the war, it became a high-profile moment in Colombia’s long struggle to move from armed confrontation toward negotiation — a message Karina herself summed up plainly: dialogue, not more bloodshed.

Karina’s surrender was seen as both a military and propaganda success for the Colombian state. *By [Reporter Name], CNN-style news report*

**Bogotá, Colombia** — After nearly a quarter-century in the ranks of Colombia’s FARC guerrillas, a female commander has abandoned the rebel group, surrendering to authorities and beginning the uncertain path toward civilian life.

Colombian military officials said the woman, who had spent 24 years with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, turned herself in after months of increased pressure from security forces in a region where dissident and remaining armed groups continue to operate. Her identity has not been fully disclosed, authorities said, due to concerns for her safety and the possibility of retaliation.

The former commander is now expected to enter a government reintegration program designed for ex-combatants who lay down their weapons. Such programs typically offer psychological support, education, job training and assistance reconnecting with family members — but the transition is often difficult, especially for former fighters who spent much of their lives inside a guerrilla hierarchy.

“She is afraid,” a military official familiar with the case said. “Not only because of what she left behind, but because leaving the group can be seen as betrayal.”

The FARC, once Latin America’s largest guerrilla army, signed a landmark peace agreement with the Colombian government in 2016, formally ending more than five decades of conflict. Thousands of fighters demobilized under the accord. But several factions rejected the deal or later returned to arms, citing insecurity, slow implementation of rural reforms and disputes over illegal economies, including drug trafficking and mining.

Women played significant roles within the FARC’s military and political structures, serving as combatants, intelligence operatives, medics and commanders. For many, reintegration presents distinct challenges, including trauma, stigma, separation from children or families, and fear of gender-based violence.

Colombia’s armed forces have intensified operations against armed groups in recent years, targeting guerrilla commanders, supply routes and illegal financing networks. Officials say that pressure has contributed to defections, as lower- and mid-level members become increasingly isolated and concerned about survival.

Human rights groups, however, warn that military pressure alone cannot resolve the underlying problems fueling Colombia’s conflict. Rural poverty, weak state presence, land disputes and the expansion of illicit economies continue to create conditions in which armed groups recruit and operate.

For the former commander, the immediate concern is safety. Authorities said she is receiving protection while officials evaluate possible threats against her. Former combatants who abandon armed groups can face reprisals from former comrades, rival factions or criminal organizations that fear they may provide intelligence to the government.

Reintegration specialists say the first months after surrender are critical.

“Leaving an armed group is not a single event,” one expert said. “It is a long process of rebuilding identity, trust and basic life skills. Many former combatants don’t know how to live outside the structure that controlled every part of their lives.”

Colombia’s peace process remains one of the most ambitious attempts in the world to move fighters from war into civilian society. But the assassination of social leaders and former combatants has raised persistent doubts about whether the state can guarantee security for those who disarm.

Still, officials presented the commander’s surrender as a significant blow to remaining armed factions and a sign that government pressure is working.

For the woman at the center of the case, the decision marks the end of 24 years in the jungle — and the beginning of a future filled with uncertainty.

“She wants a second chance,” the military official said. “Now the challenge is making sure she survives long enough to have one.”

*By Staff Writer*  
*Bogotá, Colombia —*

A senior commander of Colombia’s Revolutionary Armed Forces, or FARC, has surrendered to authorities, delivering another symbolic blow to the country’s largest guerrilla organization at a time when its leadership has been weakened by military pressure, desertions and internal mistrust.

The rebel, widely identified by her nom de guerre **“Karina,”** was one of the most prominent female commanders in the FARC and had operated for years in the mountainous coffee-growing region of western Colombia. Colombian officials said her demobilization reflected growing pressure inside the guerrilla ranks and renewed their call for other insurgents to lay down their arms and return to civilian life.

Karina, whose real name has been reported as **Elda Neyis Mosquera García**, was accused by authorities of participating in kidnappings, attacks on civilians and killings during her years as a commander in the FARC’s regional structures. Her surrender comes amid a broader campaign by the Colombian government to encourage rebel demobilization through offers of legal benefits, protection and reintegration support.

Government officials presented the surrender as evidence that the guerrilla group—already shaken by major battlefield losses—was becoming increasingly isolated.

“Those still in the jungle should understand that there is a path back,” officials said in public appeals following the demobilization. The government urged rank-and-file rebels to abandon their units, turn over weapons and take advantage of state programs designed to help former combatants reintegrate into society.

## A blow to a compartmentalized rebel structure

Founded in 1964, the FARC developed over decades into a highly structured Marxist guerrilla movement that financed itself through kidnapping, extortion, illegal mining and, according to Colombian and U.S. authorities, the drug trade. At its height, the organization fielded thousands of fighters and controlled or influenced large swaths of rural Colombia.

One reason the FARC endured for so long was its **compartmentalized command system**. Fighters were organized into fronts, columns and mobile units, often operating in remote regions with limited knowledge of other units’ activities. Commanders used couriers, coded communications and strict internal discipline to reduce the impact of captures or desertions.

That compartmentalization made the group difficult to infiltrate, but it also bred distrust. As the Colombian military expanded intelligence operations and targeted rebel leaders, communications among units became more dangerous. Government officials say some commanders increasingly feared betrayal by their own fighters, while younger guerrillas found themselves cut off from families and supplies.

Karina’s surrender, analysts said, carried importance not only because of her rank but because regional commanders often served as the connective tissue between the FARC’s top leadership and its armed fronts. When such figures defect, they can provide intelligence on hideouts, supply routes, internal discipline and the morale of fighters still in the field.

## Ivan Rios’ killing intensified mistrust

Karina’s demobilization followed another severe shock to the guerrilla hierarchy: the killing of **Iván Ríos**, a member of the FARC’s ruling Secretariat.

Ríos was killed in 2008 by one of his own security men, who then approached authorities with evidence of the death. The killing stunned Colombians not only because Ríos was one of the highest-ranking rebels ever eliminated, but because he was not killed in a conventional military operation. Instead, his death exposed the internal fractures that had opened under sustained military pressure and the government’s rewards program.

The episode sent a message through the guerrilla ranks: even senior commanders surrounded by loyal guards were vulnerable. For the government, it became proof that the FARC’s internal cohesion was weakening. For rebels in the field, it deepened suspicions that comrades could become informants or defectors.

The death of Ríos came during a period of repeated setbacks for the FARC. Earlier, Colombian forces had carried out operations against top commanders and increased pressure on encampments. The military also expanded broadcasts, leaflet drops and family-contact campaigns urging rebels to desert.

## Victims demand truth and accountability

For victims of FARC violence, the surrender of a senior rebel commander brought mixed emotions: relief that a feared figure was no longer in the field, but also anger and a demand for justice.

Human rights advocates and victims’ organizations have long insisted that demobilization must not mean silence. They argue that former commanders should provide full accounts of kidnappings, disappearances, forced recruitment, land mines and attacks on villages.

One victim from the coffee-growing region where Karina operated recalled years of fear under guerrilla influence. Families, community leaders and small business owners often faced extortion demands or threats, while those suspected of cooperating with the state risked retaliation.

Victims have called on authorities to ensure that any legal benefits offered to demobilized rebels are tied to cooperation with investigations, reparations and the recovery of truth. Many families still do not know where missing relatives were buried or who ordered specific attacks.

In communities affected by decades of war, the surrender of a commander can reopen old wounds. Some residents view demobilization as a chance for answers; others worry that former combatants may receive leniency while civilians continue to suffer the consequences of violence.

## Government presses demobilization strategy

Colombia’s government has promoted demobilization as a key part of its counterinsurgency strategy. Officials say thousands of guerrillas and militia members have abandoned armed groups over the years, often citing hunger, illness, fear of combat, separation from family and disillusionment with rebel leadership.

The state’s reintegration programs typically offer food, shelter, psychological care, education, job training and legal guidance, though the exact benefits depend on the individual’s role and pending criminal cases. Authorities have also used testimony from demobilized fighters to locate camps, weapons caches and kidnapping victims.

Following Karina’s surrender, officials again appealed directly to FARC members.

“The message is clear: demobilize before it is too late,” government representatives said, framing surrender as a safer alternative to death in combat or prosecution after capture.

The government’s message was aimed particularly at lower-ranking fighters, many of whom joined as teenagers or were recruited in rural zones with little state presence. Officials argued that the collapse or capture of commanders leaves ordinary guerrillas exposed and expendable.

## A symbolic moment in a long conflict

Karina’s demobilization was not expected to end the conflict by itself. At the time, the FARC still maintained armed units, hostages and territorial influence in several regions. But the surrender of a well-known commander reinforced the perception that the balance of power had shifted.

For Colombia’s armed forces, it was another sign that pressure on the FARC’s leadership was producing results. For the guerrillas, it underscored the danger of isolation and internal betrayal. For victims, it raised a more difficult question: whether those who once commanded fear would now help reveal the truth.

As the government urged rebels to abandon the fight, communities scarred by the conflict waited to see whether demobilization would bring not only fewer guns in the mountains, but also justice for the crimes committed there.
